article.title: Why Survivorship Bias Makes Successful Cases Look More Typical Than They Are
article.why: 理解只觀察留下來的案例如何扭曲成功率與因果敘事。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Survivorship bias appears when analysis focuses on the cases that remain visible while ignoring the cases that disappeared. Because failures, dropouts, closures, and abandoned strategies are often harder to observe, successful examples can look more common and more typical than they really are.

Imagine studying entrepreneurs by interviewing only founders who still run successful companies. You may discover that many of them took large risks, worked extremely long hours, and ignored early criticism. It would be tempting to conclude that these behaviors are reliable causes of success. But many failed founders may have done exactly the same things. If they are missing from the sample, the analysis overstates how informative those behaviors are.

The same problem appears in investing. Looking only at funds that exist today can make historical performance seem stronger because poorly performing funds may have closed or merged. In product analytics, studying only active users can hide the experience of people who churned. In hiring, examining only employees who stayed for several years can miss characteristics of those who left early.

The mechanism is selection. Survival is not random. Whether a case remains observable is often related to the outcome being studied. That means the visible sample is filtered by a process that can distort averages, correlations, and stories.

One warning sign is language such as ‘all successful companies do X’ when the comparison group is unclear. The missing question is: how many unsuccessful companies also did X? A practice can be common among winners and still have little predictive value if it is equally common among losers.

To reduce survivorship bias, analysts should define the original population before looking at outcomes. If possible, include closed businesses, churned customers, rejected applications, discontinued products, and other cases that disappeared from the current database. Historical snapshots can help because current systems often overwrite or remove inactive records.

Sometimes the missing cases cannot be recovered. Then the limitation should be stated explicitly. Sensitivity analysis can also help. Analysts can ask how conclusions would change if the unseen group had systematically worse outcomes.

Survivorship bias also affects qualitative learning. Case studies are memorable because success creates documentation, interviews, books, and conference talks. Failure often leaves less evidence. This creates an information environment in which success stories are overrepresented even before any formal analysis begins.

A classic way to think about the problem is to ask, ‘What had to happen for this observation to become visible to me?’ That question shifts attention from the observed sample to the selection process.

Suppose a company wants to learn why long-term customers are loyal. Interviewing only current customers may identify useful habits, but it cannot fully explain retention. The company should also examine customers who looked similar at the start but later left. The contrast between survivors and non-survivors is often where the most useful insight appears.

Survivorship bias does not make successful cases useless. Successful examples can still teach mechanisms, tactics, and possibilities. The danger comes from treating them as representative without checking who is missing.

In business analysis, the safest habit is simple: whenever a dataset contains only people, products, or companies that are still present, ask whether disappearance was related to performance. If it was, the visible sample may tell a systematically optimistic story. A complete denominator matters. Before comparing success rates, reconstruct who entered the process, who exited, and why those exits became invisible.
paragraphs.zh: 倖存者偏差來自只看仍然可見的成功者或留下者，而忽略退出、失敗與被移除的案例。分析前要先還原原始母體與完整 denominator，確認『消失』本身是否和結果相關。

quiz.question: Why do successful cases look more typical under survivorship bias?
quiz.answer: Because failed or disappeared cases are missing from the observed sample.

quiz.question: What should analysts reconstruct first?
quiz.answer: The original population and the cases that exited.
